query: Earlier W-based high-entropy alloys showed promising microstructural stability, high-temperature strength, and irradiation tolerance, but most contained Nb, Mo, Cr, or Ni, whose activation behavior and other service limitations restrict their suitability for plasma-facing components. Candidate structural materials must combine thermal and mechanical performance with low neutron activation and rapid radioactive decay. The equimolar WTaTiVZr alloy uses refractory, relatively low-activation constituents and has shown creep and molten-salt-corrosion resistance, yet its plastic strain and toughness remain unreported and poorly understood. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs its plastic strain and toughness relative to commercially used pure tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing-component service? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the hypothesized cause, the observations predicted relative to pure tungsten, the boundaries of validity, the cited prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The enhanced plastic strain and toughness of the equimolar WTaTiVZr alloy relative to pure tungsten under high‐temperature plasma‐facing service is governed by an increase in grain boundary cohesion due to the segregation of Ti and Zr. These elements lower the grain boundary energy, mitigate crack initiation, and promote more uniform dislocation activity, thereby facilitating ductile, grain-boundary‐mediated deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar WTaTiVZr processed into a fine-grained microstructure with uniformly distributed refractory elements; compared to commercially used polycrystalline pure tungsten.
generation.intervention: Subject both the WTaTiVZr alloy and pure tungsten samples to identical high-temperature mechanical tests (e.g., tensile/creep tests) under controlled strain rate and environmental conditions that simulate plasma-facing service.
generation.conditions: High-temperature environment (approximately 1000–1600 K) and stress regimes relevant to plasma-facing components, ensuring identical loading and thermal exposure for both materials.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary regions enriched in Ti and Zr.
generation.mechanism: Ti and Zr preferentially segregate to the grain boundaries in the alloy, reducing the interfacial energy and increasing cohesion. This enhanced cohesion reduces intergranular crack propagation and supports grain boundary sliding coupled with dislocation motion, resulting in increased plastic deformation and improved toughness. In contrast, pure tungsten, lacking such segregation, is more prone to brittle intergranular cracking under similar conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature mechanical loading, the WTaTiVZr alloy will exhibit higher plastic strain (more ductile behavior) and a greater toughness margin (delayed crack initiation/propagation) compared to pure tungsten. Microstructural analyses should reveal Ti and Zr enrichment at the grain boundaries and evidence of grain-boundary-mediated deformation.
generation.baseline: Pure tungsten typically shows limited plastic strain and low toughness under high-temperature conditions due to rapid crack initiation at grain boundaries leading to brittle failure.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be operative within the temperature and stress conditions typical for plasma-facing components (around 1000–1600 K). It may not apply in regimes where other deformation mechanisms dominate (e.g., at cryogenic temperatures or extreme ultra-high temperatures).
generation.uncertainty: While grain boundary segregation is a plausible mechanism, the precise quantitative contribution of this effect relative to potential intragranular dislocation dynamics is not fully established. The kinetics of segregation and possible formation of interfacial precipitates may also influence the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare equimolar WTaTiVZr and pure tungsten samples with comparable grain sizes, then perform high-temperature tensile or creep tests under identical conditions. Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atom probe tomography (APT) to analyze grain boundary chemistry. Compare stress–strain curves, fracture surfaces, and evidence of grain-boundary slip or decohesion.
measurements: Stress–strain curves to determine plastic strain and toughness metrics
TEM and APT analyses to verify Ti and Zr enrichment at grain boundaries
Fractography for observing intergranular versus transgranular fracture behavior
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the WTaTiVZr alloy does not show significantly enhanced plastic strain or toughness compared to pure tungsten, or if microstructural characterization fails to detect meaningful Ti and Zr segregation at grain boundaries contributing to cohesion, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [ [1] ], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years [ [2] ]. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co [ [3] ].

First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [ [4] , [5] ]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [6] ]. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [ [7] ] and yield strength σ 0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa [ [5] ].
